Joel-Peter Witkin has spent five decades building elaborately staged photographs that look like they were unearthed from some forgotten wing of art history — tableaux populated by cadavers, amputees, hermaphrodites, and other figures excluded from conventional pictures of beauty, arranged with the same compositional seriousness Velázquez or Goya brought to a royal court. What makes the work more than shock value is the craft underneath it. Witkin doesn't just photograph his tableaux — he attacks the negative and print afterward, scratching the emulsion, bleaching sections, sometimes drawing directly on the surface, so that each finished piece sits somewhere between photograph and hand-worked object. The pictures reference Picasso, Courbet, and Christian iconography as often as they reference the darkroom, and the effect is a body of work that treats mortality and the marginalized body as subjects worthy of the grandest possible visual language.

This show is a fitting occasion: a chance to see a genuinely singular, still-controversial photographic practice presented with the scholarly care usually reserved for painting retrospectives.

Rahim Fortune's black-and-white photographs read like a long, unhurried conversation with the American South. Working across Texas and Oklahoma, where he grew up in the Chickasaw Nation, Fortune trains his camera on Black communities, church parades, family kitchens, and the land itself, treating landscape and portraiture as inseparable parts of the same story. The exhibition also debuts new color photographs and a short film Fortune made in response to the Texas African American Photography Archive, giving the show a second register alongside the black-and-white work: archival material reanimated through a contemporary lens. Organized by the Center for Photography at Woodstock and co-presented with the California African American Museum, the show runs concurrently with a companion exhibition of archive selections, so visitors effectively get two conversations about Black Texan life in one visit.

This is Fortune's first solo exhibition in Los Angeles, a notable milestone for a photographer who has quickly built a reputation for tender, unsentimental documentary work. Seeing the prints at scale, in a space designed for close looking, is a very different experience than seeing them reproduced in a book — worth the trip to Leimert Park on that basis alone.

Marking what would have been Ed Moses's hundredth year, William Turner Gallery has assembled a focused survey of paintings that trace the restless, decades-long experimentation of one of Los Angeles's founding postwar artists. Moses came up through the legendary Ferus Gallery circle alongside Robert Irwin, Ed Ruscha, and Billy Al Bengston, but unlike many of his peers he never settled into a single signature style — the show's selection, drawn from series with names like Roses, Wedges, Crackles, and Waterfalls, makes that restlessness the whole point.

What comes through in these canvases is less a fixed "look" than a working method: Moses treated painting as a physical, almost ritual practice, one he described as trying to be "in tune" rather than in control. He kept at it in his Venice studio until his death in 2018 at ninety-one, and the works on view here — bold, gestural, materially varied — reflect an artist who kept mutating his own vocabulary well into old age.

It's a good one to catch before it closes September 5.

Judy Baca's half-mile mural along the Tujunga Wash is the longest in the world, and this section extends its chronology of California social history into the Reagan era: the rise of Reaganomics and its role in deepening wealth inequality and homelessness, the Free South Africa divestment movement, the War on Drugs and mass incarceration, the emergence of punk, rap and hip-hop as vehicles of dissent, the AIDS crisis, and grassroots organizing by women of color and Central American refugees fleeing US-backed conflicts.

Rather than showing only finished panels, SPARC's Bergamot gallery presentation pairs mural segments with studies, transfer drawings and color renderings, pulling back the curtain on the collaborative, years-long process of building a public monument of this scale. It's a rare chance to see the working materials behind one of Los Angeles's most significant pieces of civic art up close, rather than from a car window along the flood channel.

For anyone who has only encountered the Great Wall as a drive-by landmark, this show recontextualizes it as an evolving, still-growing archive of grassroots memory — one that SPARC and Baca's Great Wall Institute intend to extend to a full mile by the 2028 Olympics. The Bergamot space itself gives the mural room to be studied as art rather than just passed by.

Alfredo Ramos Martínez is often called the father of Mexican Modernism — he mentored David Alfaro Siqueiros and Rufino Tamayo and pushed a generation of painters out of the studio and into the landscape. This exhibition, drawn from the artist's estate, gathers tempera-on-paper and oil landscapes made after his 1929 move to Los Angeles, when homesickness for Mexico's mountains and markets became a lifelong subject.

The show's anchor works trace a single mental thread: the Cordillera, the mountain spine that runs from the Sierra Madre down through the Americas. Martínez's Cordillera Mexicana pays tribute to the Sierra Madre Oriental peaks above his native Monterrey, while other paintings place indigenous women bearing flowers and produce beneath the volcanoes ringing the Valley of Mexico. Even his delicate studies of floripondio blossoms — a South American flower he found growing as an ornamental in both Mexico and Southern California — read as a metaphor for his own transplanted life.

It's a quieter, more historical show than most of what's on view in LA's contemporary-leaning galleries right now, but a good one for anyone curious about the roots of Mexican modernism as seen from Los Angeles, a city where Martínez spent his final two decades and where his legacy is held in depth at LACMA and beyond.

Marilyn Monroe has been photographed more than almost any other human being, and this group show at Peter Fetterman assembles the work of the photographers who actually stood in the room with her — Eve Arnold, Henri Cartier-Bresson, Cornell Capa, Elliott Erwitt, Philippe Halsman, Douglas Kirkland, Bert Stern, Sam Shaw, George Barris, Andre de Dienes, Milton H. Greene and others. Rather than the tabloid iconography most people carry around in their heads, the prints here lean toward the quieter, more observational end of the spectrum: Monroe resting between takes on the set of "The Misfits," going over lines in the Nevada desert, or caught mid-laugh at the Actors Studio.

Because so many of these photographers were friends or colleagians of Monroe rather than paparazzi, the exhibition reads less like a celebrity retrospective and more like a study of trust between subject and camera. Bert Stern's "Last Sitting" images, made just weeks before her death, sit alongside Cartier-Bresson's spare reportage from the set of "The Misfits" and Andre de Dienes's early, unguarded pictures of her near Malibu in 1946 — a useful reminder that her image was constructed over more than fifteen years by dozens of different eyes.

The range of processes on view — gelatin silver prints, platinum/palladium prints, and archival pigment estate prints spanning the 1940s through the 1960s — traces the material history behind these images. For anyone interested in mid-century photojournalism as much as in Monroe herself, it's a rich survey of how the top photographers of the era approached a single, endlessly complicated subject.

Roger Herman has been a fixture of Los Angeles painting since the late 1970s, and this show finds the German-born, UCLA-affiliated artist doing what he does best: turning flowers, mountains, and skulls into loose, saturated fields of brushwork that refuse to sit still. The poppy paintings are the emotional center — layered, almost gaudy stacks of leaf and petal built from dashes and smears rather than careful description — while a companion landscape painting renders a mountain in broad strokes of blue, turquoise, and white.

What makes the show more than a painting survey is the ceramics. Herman throws large, irregular vessels on the wheel and then treats the glazing the way he treats a canvas, letting color pool and shift unpredictably across the surface. A dining table and coffee table extend that same logic into furniture, their tops built from painterly ceramic panels, and a set of tiny mezcal cups modeled on the traditional jicara round out the display at a much more intimate scale.

Pairing an untidy, expressionist painter like Herman with this gallery is a smart bit of counter-programming — proof that the gallery's West Hollywood outpost isn't just showing polished design pieces but also giving space to an artist whose work resists polish on principle.

Yoko Ono's first solo museum survey in Southern California treats her not as John Lennon's collaborator but as the conceptual artist she was well before the Beatles ever met her: a key figure in Fluxus whose instruction pieces, films, and participatory works helped invent the idea that an artwork could be something a visitor completes rather than just looks at. The Broad's presentation spans seven decades, from spare 1960s text works to the immersive, hands-on installations she's best known for today.

That participatory streak is the heart of the show. Visitors are invited to tie a wish to an olive tree, hammer a nail into a painting, write a note to their mother and pin it to a wall, or add a stroke of blue marker to a boat-shaped sculpture representing displacement and refuge. Alongside these interactive works are historical touchstones like "Cut Piece" and "Fly," which show Ono working through vulnerability, gender, and the body decades before those became gallery-standard subjects.

It's a rare chance to see Ono treated with full institutional weight rather than as a footnote to rock history, and the hands-on nature of the work makes it one of the more genuinely fun, all-ages museum visits in the city right now.

The show also includes small collaborative sculptures, including a modified microwave mounted on a motorized plinth, and a series of Mitchell's graphite drawings that catalogue the same charged, generic vocabulary — Crying, Molesting, Gossip, Spanking — in a schoolbook hand. The show is shown alongside its companion exhibition The Cars of Los Angeles.

This exhibition draws on the Texas African American Photography Archive to reconstruct a visual record of Black life in small towns and rural communities across eastern Texas between 1944 and 1984. The photographs are the work of local studio photographers who spent careers documenting their own neighborhoods rather than working for outside publications, and the result is an intimate, unglamorous archive of portraits, church gatherings, rodeos, parades, school pictures, and family celebrations.

What makes the material compelling is its scale and specificity: this isn't a survey of famous images but a deep well of vernacular photography, much of which has never been widely seen and a great deal of similar material from the era has simply been lost. Seen together, the pictures trace four decades that span the height of Jim Crow segregation through the civil rights era, without editorializing — the politics are present in the everyday texture of the images rather than in overt protest photography.

The show is organized by the Center for Photography at Woodstock and curated by Nicole R. Fleetwood, a scholar whose research often centers marginalized visual archives. It's presented at Art + Practice. For anyone interested in photography as community record-keeping rather than fine-art spectacle, this is a rewarding, quietly moving show.

Taix French Restaurant sat on Sunset Boulevard in Echo Park for nearly a century before it closed and was gutted for redevelopment, and this show is essentially six photographers and one mixed-media artist working through what that kind of loss looks like. Maxfield Hegedus shot the interior room by room before demolition — bar, ballroom, dining room, both bathrooms, the private room — turning a beloved but unglamorous restaurant into a document of a particular strain of mid-century LA design. The show nods explicitly to Ed Ruscha's "Every Building on the Sunset Strip," and that reference gives the whole project its logic: this is vernacular architecture photography as elegy, cataloguing a stretch of the city's built environment right before it disappears. Evan Whale's altered c-print, carved and chemigrammed until the image partially dissolves into smoke and texture, is the most physically worked-over piece in the show and a good counterpoint to the more straightforward documentary images around it.

This show uses a single closed restaurant as a lens onto memory, urban change, and the particular melancholy of watching a familiar place get erased.

This photography show pulls together seven photographers — Deborah Feingold, Gary Heery, Jack Lue, Marc Canter, Mark Weiss, Mick Rock, and Richard Corman — who were in the room during those first five years, from club gigs and cassette-tape hustling to the arena-scale Like a Virgin tour of 1985.

What comes through across the prints is less a chronicle of stardom than a document of instinct: Madonna turning down a packaged pop career in Paris to keep creative control, bringing demos straight to New York DJs instead of waiting for a label, and treating her collaborators — photographers, stylists, dancers — as co-authors of a visual identity rather than hired help. In the 1980s, Nicolae Ceaușescu's "systematization" campaign flattened roughly a third of historic Bucharest to make way for the oversized avenues and government buildings of a totalitarian regime. Seven churches, deemed too significant to destroy outright, were instead jacked up, set on rails, and physically wheeled behind new apartment blocks — hidden in plain sight rather than demolished. Photographer Anton Roland Laub, who grew up amid this leveled cityscape, spent years tracking down these displaced structures and documenting how they sit today, wedged into gaps between mismatched postwar architecture.

The exhibition — Laub's first solo presentation in the United States — pairs his contemporary large-format photographs with archival material from the era of the relocations, including material from the engineer who devised the rail-lifting technique. The pictures are quiet and procedural rather than sensational: facades caught at odd angles against concrete housing, empty lots where history was erased, buildings that look stranded rather than saved. Together they form a document of a strange, little-known act of architectural survival under one of Eastern Europe's most destructive dictatorships.

This is the first chapter of a three-part project by Laub examining the final years of the Ceaușescu regime, continued in his later series Last Christmas (of Ceaușescu) and Mineriada. Guest-curated by independent curator Sonia Voss, the show rewards a slow look at how state power reshapes — and sometimes just relocates — the physical fabric of a city.

Timed to land on the 250th anniversary of the United States, this group exhibition turns a skeptical eye on the myths nations tell about their own founding. Beverly Art Boutique's standing exhibition gathers work spanning the long career of Revington Arthur (1908–1986), an American painter, educator, and print-world organizer who trained at the Art Students League under teachers including Arshile Gorky and George Luks. The gallery draws on a large estate holding of more than 700 original works, letting visitors trace Arthur's evolution from nature studies and figurative American-scene painting toward the hard-edged, primary-colored geometric abstraction he developed in the 1950s and after, much of it inflected by the era's fascination with space travel and technology.

What's on the walls ranges from early lyrical landscapes and lifestyle scenes to the later non-objective compositions built from interlocking geometric shapes — canvases that read as a personal register of mid-century American formal experimentation, made by a painter who spent decades teaching as much as exhibiting. Arthur also founded the Chautauqua Art Center and co-founded the New England and National Print Show, and his paintings entered the collections of institutions such as the Brooklyn Museum, the Walker Art Center, and the Albright-Knox (now Buffalo AKG).

Several of the artists included — Eiko Yamazawa, Aiko Miyawaki, Etsuko Nakatsuji, Shizuko Yoshikawa — also worked as graphic designers, and the show argues that this dual practice sharpened rather than diluted their formal thinking, feeding a shared interest in order and non-psychological composition. The centerpiece is reportedly Madani's most ambitious video to date, an animated work built from painted, drawn, and photographed source material and scored by artist Nathaniel Mellors, in which renegade letters of the alphabet escape the page and start remaking the world in their own image — a fable about language, domination, and the way symbols calcify into systems of control. Kintsugi — the practice of repairing broken ceramics with gold-dusted lacquer — has become such a popular metaphor in wellness culture that it's easy to forget the actual objects behind it: centuries-old tea bowls whose cracks were mended rather than hidden, turning damage into ornament. This group show at JACCC's Doizaki Gallery, curated by Japanese art historian Meher McArthur, puts those historical vessels in the same room as more than thirty contemporary works that take the kintsugi philosophy in far more varied directions.

The exhibition is organized in three parts, moving from the traditional tea-ceremony roots of gold lacquer repair through contemporary artists actively practicing the technique on ceramics, and finally to work that borrows kintsugi's logic — visible repair as a form of beauty — for painting, sculpture, textile art and installation. Artists in the show include Miya Ando, Naoko Fukumaru, Ted Meyer and Kristine Schomaker, among others, several of whom have used the idea of "golden repair" to address illness, grief, or trauma rather than literal broken pottery.

It's a modest but well-considered survey of an idea that gets invoked constantly and examined rarely — a chance to see where the actual craft tradition ends and the metaphor begins. Carl Cheng has been quietly making some of Los Angeles's most prescient art since the 1960s, and this survey — the first to trace his full six-decade career — finally gives him the wide-lens treatment. This is a focused historical survey of the earliest, most experimental years of Keith Sonnier's career, honing in on 1968 to 1970, when the Louisiana-born artist first began bending neon and argon gas into sculpture. Sonnier, who died in 2020, is remembered as one of the great postwar American sculptors, and this show captures the moment he found his signature material: glowing tube light paired with the raw fixtures, transformers, and wiring that power it. Works like the two-tone "Arced Neon" pieces from 1968 show him testing single gestures in colored light, while the later, more elaborate "Neon Wrapping Incandescent V" (1970) shows a fast-maturing vocabulary of layered, multicolor form.

What makes this body of work compelling beyond its historical importance is how physical it still feels — these are sculptures that depend on their walls and corners the way a painting depends on its stretcher bars, casting shadow and colored light into the room and implicating the viewer's own silhouette in the composition. Sonnier arrived at these ideas while still a student, in dialogue with contemporaries like Eva Hesse and Bruce Nauman, and this exhibition makes the case for how radical that dialogue with industrial materials and immaterial light really was.

It's a tightly scoped, jewel-box kind of show rather than a full retrospective, but for anyone interested in postminimalism, the history of light as sculptural material, or just wanting to see real neon glow in person, it's worth the visit.

Anida Yoeu Ali's long-running performance project centers on a single, unforgettable image: a nearly 328-foot saffron-colored creature with a human face wrapped tightly in cloth at one end and a pair of bare feet at the other. The robe-like orange skin nods to Buddhist monastic dress, while the fabric framing the Bug's face recalls the hijab, a deliberate collision of religious and cultural signifiers that keeps the work from settling into any single reading. It's a costume, a performance vehicle, and a kind of wandering monument to displacement and belonging all at once.

Todd Gray has spent the past decade building large-scale photographic assemblages that layer images of European palaces, museums, and churches against sites tied to the transatlantic slave trade on the West African coast, interspersed with pictures of Black cultural icons pulled from his own archive. The circular, sculpturally framed photographs, often stacked in clusters, ask viewers to hold two histories of Western wealth and Black cultural production in the same frame at once.

This exhibition at The Brick pairs three of those assemblages, including two new mural-scale works, with an unusual amount of biographical material: photographs and ephemera from Gray's own life as a teenager who shot The Rolling Stones and Led Zeppelin around Los Angeles before becoming Michael Jackson's personal photographer and, eventually, a CalArts-trained fine artist alongside classmates like Mike Kelley and Carrie Mae Weems. Seeing the commercial photography and the gallery practice side by side clarifies how much one fed the other.

Organized by the Brick's director Hamza Walker, the show doubles as the occasion for a forthcoming book of an extended interview between the two. For anyone who has only encountered Gray's assemblages in isolation, this is a rare chance to see the life that produced them.

Ann Leda Shapiro has spent five decades making watercolors and works on paper that treat the body as a landscape of feeling — skin standing in for terrain, internal organs rendered as weather systems, psychological states given physical form. Her paintings move fluidly between the anatomical and the cosmic: a "Bonded Bodies" composition, a smoke-veiled tree at the edge of a fire, a spine drawn like a coiled snake. There's a loose, watery immediacy to her line that owes something to both feminist body art of the 1970s and older traditions of visionary and medical illustration.

"Through the Tunnel" gathers work spanning from the 1970s through her recent wildfire and tree paintings, tracing a long arc in which the personal (illness, aging, grief) keeps bumping up against the environmental (drought, fire, loss of habitat). Titles like "Smoke from Wildfires" and "Tornado" sit alongside earlier, more intimate pieces such as "Intestinal Distress" and "Holding On," suggesting a practice that has always used the body to talk about the world, and vice versa.

It's a chance to see how a career built on unguarded, visceral image-making holds up against, and speaks to, the present moment.

Tomatâ du Plenty was best known as the wild-eyed frontman of The Screamers, the confrontational synth-punk band that never released a studio album yet became one of the most mythologized acts to come out of the late-1970s Hollywood punk scene. Less known is that he was also a working visual artist, and this show at MutMuz Gallery gathers a cross-section of that largely unseen body of work.

The exhibition brings together multimedia paintings on wood, works on paper, photographs, and ephemera pulled from du Plenty's archive, giving a sense of an artist whose visual language was as unruly and theatrical as his stage persona. Expect handmade, collaged, and painted objects rather than a polished studio practice — the kind of work that reads as diary, prop, and provocation all at once, in keeping with the anarchic performance-art roots he shared with Screamers bandmates and the broader Hollywood underground of that era.

For longtime devotees of The Screamers and LA punk history this is a rare chance to see du Plenty's actual hand at work rather than just photographs of his performances; for newcomers it's an entry point into a figure who looms large in punk mythology but left behind surprisingly little visual record until now. The show runs through mid-September in MutMuz's compact Chung King Road storefront.

Carmen Amengual's installation reworks a piece she first made in 2024 — a multichannel video originally commissioned by Prospect Art — into a denser meditation on how political power colonizes language. Words like "life," "freedom," and "memory" get staged and restaged in short, deliberately crude scenes that borrow from black-light theater, shadow puppetry, and early cinema, a visual language chosen precisely because it's technologically modest and a little absurd against such heavy subject matter.

Two suspended sculptures extend the video's argument into physical space: mobile forms built from ceramic, wood, and leather strap spelling out cursive phrases — "Dismembered by Capital" and "Disembodied by Intelligence" — that double as research objects, since Amengual built them after studying medieval instruments of restraint and discipline. The body implied throughout is left ambiguous on purpose, read as individual, collective, or civic depending on where you're standing.

Amengual is an Argentine-born artist and researcher (CalArts MFA, Whitney ISP alum) whose work usually starts from buried archival material — here, an unrealized documentary project tied to the 1970s Third World Filmmakers Meetings feeds into her broader interest in how resistance movements get remembered, forgotten, and rewritten. This is dense, research-driven work, well suited to the kind of space that gives it room to breathe.
